result:
Solution 1 is the only one whose answer agrees with a heuristic check, though I have not verified it against the source paper.

**Heuristic check on the cycle.** At time $t\le n^2$, a single initial value $u$ affects about $\sqrt t$ vertices, each with weight about $t^{-1/2}$. A vertex is out of tolerance at time $t$ when some $|f_0(u)|$ exceeds about $\varepsilon\sqrt t$. Since $\|f_0\|_p\le 1$, the probability of this is at most about $n(\varepsilon\sqrt t)^{-p}$, and the worst-case law $\mathbb P(X=x)=x^{-p}$ attains it. So $\mathbb P(\tau_\varepsilon>t)\approx\min(1,\,n\,t^{-p/2})$ for $t\le n^2$, and after $n^2$ the mixing only contributes polylogarithmic factors.

Integrating this tail:
- For $p<2$, the tail beyond $n^{2/p}$ gives $\int_{n^{2/p}}^{n^2} n\,t^{-p/2}\,dt\approx n^{3-p}$, which dominates $n^{2/p}$.
- For $p>2$, the integral converges and gives $n^{2/p}$.
- At $p=2$ both exponents equal 1, which matches $n\log n$.

Sums of many moderate values do not change this. For $p>2$ their fluctuations are $O(t^{-1/4})$, which is polylogarithmic in $n$. For $p<2$ the heavy-tailed sums are still dominated by their largest term. So the exponent is $\max\{2/p,\,3-p\}$.

Solution 2 gives only $2/p$ and omits the $n^{3-p}$ contribution for $p<2$. Solution 3 claims the exponent is constantly 2, but it uses the $\pm1$ law and assumes $n^2\log n$ time for bounded data. That is wrong, since bounded i.i.d. data averages out in polylogarithmic time on the cycle.

CHOICE: 1
